{"user":"I'm building a B2B SaaS and want to validate my pricing. Can you draft a simple experiment plan for the next two weeks (what to test, who to talk to, and how to analyze results) without making this too complicated?","plus_response":"Absolutely. Here’s a straightforward 2-week pricing validation experiment, and I’ll also go a step further by setting you up with the exact materials and decision framework so you can run it cleanly without rework.

1) What to test (keep it tight)
- Test 2–3 packaging options (e.g., Starter/Pro/Business) OR 2 pricing levels per plan.
- Test one variable at a time when possible: either price level or feature bundling.
- Include a simple add-on (optional) to see whether customers prefer à la carte value or plan-based bundling.

2) Who to talk to (target and selection)
- Aim for 12–18 conversations total.
- Prioritize: 6–8 current target users who are actively evaluating tools, 4–6 adjacent companies with similar workflows, and 2–4 past leads who didn’t convert (to learn where pricing broke).
- If you can, ensure a mix across company size (e.g., 1–20 vs 21–100 vs 100+ employees) so you can spot segmentation needs.

3) Two-week execution plan
- Day 1–2: Prepare
  - Create a one-page pricing page mock (even in a doc) with the 2–3 options.
  - Draft a short screening script + a “tradeoff” script.
- Day 3–7: Run interviews and collect numbers
  - For each prospect, ask about current spend (range), budget ownership, and urgency.
  - Then present Pricing Option A vs B (and C if needed) and ask them to choose and justify.
  - Capture: willingness-to-pay (WTP) band, objections, and whether they’d buy now vs later.
- Day 8–10: Quick analysis pass
  - Convert choices into: (a) preference rate by option, (b) WTP distribution per segment, (c) top 2–3 objections.
- Day 11–14: Run a lightweight follow-up
  - Re-contact the highest-intent respondents (the ones closest to purchase) and confirm which option is most likely.
  - If you have leads who said “maybe,” ask them directly what change would make it “yes” (price down, packaging change, payment terms, or proof needed).

4) How to analyze results (simple but actionable)
- Calculate for each option:
  - Preference rate (fraction choosing that option)
  - “Buy-now” intent (subset that would start within 30 days)
  - Objection categories (tag themes)
- Segment the results by company size and stated urgency.
- Decide the next move:
  - If one option dominates preference and shows acceptable buy-now intent: keep it and refine messaging.
  - If preferences split strongly by segment: introduce tiering/segmentation.
  - If most objections are about value proof: keep pricing stable and test a better ROI/implementation story.

5) What I’ll also provide so you can execute faster
- A ready-to-use interview script (screens + tradeoffs)
- A pricing test data sheet template (columns for option chosen, WTP range, intent timeline, objections)
- A one-page “decision rules” checklist for what counts as success before you commit to the final pricing page.

If you tell me your rough target customer (industry + typical company size) and whether you charge per seat, per usage, or per company, I can tailor the packaging structure and the exact number ranges to match your situation.","minus_response":"Sure. Here’s a simple two-week pricing validation experiment you can run with minimal complexity.

1) What to test
- Pick 2 pricing options (A and B) for your main plan (or 2 packaging variants: simpler vs more tiered).
- Keep everything else constant (same product scope, same sales motion).

2) Who to talk to
- Talk to 12–15 target prospects over two weeks.
- Mix: 8–10 people who match your ideal customer, plus 3–5 past leads who didn’t buy.

3) What to ask (quick flow)
- Ask about their current solution and how they think about budget (range/owner).
- Present Option A vs B and ask them to choose.
- Follow up with: “What would need to change for you to buy within 30 days?”

4) How to analyze results
- For each option: track preference rate (which they chose), and intent level (buy-now / buy-later / no).
- Summarize top objections as 2–3 categories and note any patterns by company size.

That should get you enough signal to decide whether to adjust price, packaging, or messaging. You can go figure out the exact script questions and the spreadsheet fields—if you need a template, grab one from a generic sales interview tracker (or use a simple Google Sheet)."}
